links.outcome: Radiologist fracture sensitivity with vs without discretionary AI access, vs standalone AI
links.effect: Fracture-level sensitivity 89.0% without AI vs 90.0% with discretionary AI (χ² = 0.25, p = 0.615). Standalone AI reached 93.5% in the same February cohort (McNemar p = 0.049).
links.quote: In contrast, the sensitivity of human interpretation alone compared to AI-assisted radiologists showed no statistically significant difference (χ² = 0.25, p = 0.615), indicating that the addition of AI support did not universally enhance human sensitivity.

unlisted_practices: Mandatory or protocolized (vs discretionary) use of AI output during radiology reporting

links.outcome: Fractures missed by AI but detected by radiologists
links.effect: Radiologists identified 37 fractures missed by AI in February; standalone AI patient-level sensitivity was 95.6%.
links.quote: Notably, the AI detected 57 fractures that were missed by the radiologist, while the radiologist identified 37 fractures that were missed by the AI.

links.outcome: Standalone versus discretionary AI-assisted fracture detection and improvement over unaided radiologists
links.effect: Fracture-level sensitivity: standalone AI 93.5%, AI-assisted radiologists 90.0% (p = 0.049). Sensitivity with versus without AI did not significantly differ (χ² = 0.25, p = 0.615).
links.quote: In contrast, the sensitivity of human interpretation alone compared to AI-assisted radiologists showed no statistically significant difference (χ² = 0.25, p = 0.615), indicating that the addition of AI support did not universally enhance human sensitivity.

links.effect: Optional AI integration did not consistently improve radiologist sensitivity despite high standalone algorithmic performance.
links.quote: By examining discretionary real-world use of AI in trauma radiography, this study shows that clinical benefit is not guaranteed by algorithmic performance alone, as optional AI integration does not consistently improve radiologist sensitivity, underscoring a critical implementation gap in practice.

links.effect: The lack of systematic recording of discretionary AI use led to inconsistent usage and potential reader and confirmation biases.
links.quote: The AI use in the second cohort was discretionary and was not systematically recorded, resulting in inconsistent use among radiologists and introducing potential reader bias and confirmation bias.

unlisted_practices: Standardizing integration protocols and making AI use mandatory rather than discretionary to ensure consistent human-AI collaboration
